books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class

primary_sources: H. Leh and Company newspaper advertisement, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890

stimulus.text: The image is a newspaper advertisement headed “WE HAVE,” from H. Leh and Company of Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890. It lists pairs of ladies' and misses' shoes for sale at reduced prices, giving the old price and the new price for each lot, such as “$4.50 now $2.95.” Near the bottom it says, “Please look for stamp on bottom — Leh's Genuine Hand Sewed.” Below the shoe list, under the heading “IN RUBBER FOOTWEAR,” the firm says it carries “every style that the market affords.” The firm calls itself “Dealers in Dry Goods and Manufacturers of Boots and Shoes,” at 626, 628 and 630 Hamilton Street, Allentown, Pa.
stimulus.source_note: Newspaper advertisement for H. Leh and Company department store, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890. Public domain image from Wikimedia Commons; viewed by the writer, prices and wording read from the image.

stem: The advertisement lists old prices beside new prices, names the firm's brand stamp, and invites customers to “come and look through before your size is sold out.” Taken together, these features best illustrate which change in American retailing?

options.text: Shops stopped advertising and sold only by word of mouth
options.misconception: The ad itself is advertising; shops advertised more, not less.

options.text: Customers returned to haggling over every price
options.misconception: Printed prices replaced haggling; the ad lists fixed sale prices.

options.text: Retailing aimed at strangers, using printed prices, brands, and advertising
The government set all retail prices by law
options.misconception: No law is mentioned; the prices are the store's own.

rationales.A: This advertisement is printed in a newspaper to reach strangers. Advertising grew, it did not stop.
rationales.B: The ad prints the price for each lot. A shopper reads it instead of bargaining over it.
rationales.C: Printed prices, a brand stamp, and a newspaper invitation all speak to customers the store does not know personally. That is mass retailing.
rationales.D: The prices are set by the store and printed in its own ad. No government price-setting is shown.
rationales.general:
Put the ad's features together instead of reading one alone.
1. Printed old and new prices tell strangers what things cost without bargaining.
2. The brand stamp, “Leh's Genuine Hand Sewed,” marks the firm's goods as its own.
3. The newspaper invitation calls in customers the store has never met.
4. Background from the books: department stores built consumer culture on fixed prices, advertising, and brand names.
Remember: when several features all speak to strangers, the change is the size of the market.
